intro.title: Optics and Caustics
intro.subtitle: Interactive Optical Laboratory
intro.whatIsCaustic: What exactly is a caustic? Contrary to what it might seem, it is not a physical object, but rather a "light architecture". Derived from the Greek word kaustikos meaning "burning", it is an optical phenomenon involving the formation of bright, sharp patterns from concentrated light rays. They occur when light refracts or reflects off curved surfaces, intersecting and accumulating energy in characteristic envelopes.

snell.title: 1. Refraction (Snell's Law)
snell.theory:
Refraction is a fundamental phenomenon in geometrical optics. When a light wave passes through the boundary between two media of different optical densities, its propagation speed and direction change. The physical quantity characterizing a given medium is the index of refraction $n$ (IOR).

The mathematical model of this phenomenon is defined by Snell's Law:

$$n_1 \sin(\theta_1) = n_2 \sin(\theta_2)$$

Where $n_1$ and $n_2$ denote the refractive indices of the respective media, while $\theta_1$ and $\theta_2$ are the angles of incidence and refraction, measured relative to the normal axis (a line perpendicular to the boundary surface).
snell.descTitle: Phenomenon Analysis: Refraction and Internal Reflection
snell.descList:
The phenomenon of refraction and reflection can be analyzed by modifying the optical density of the media and the angle of incidence of the light wave:

• Refraction geometry: The passage of a ray from a less dense to a more optically dense medium (e.g., air → glass) causes the ray to bend toward the normal. In the reverse situation, the ray bends away from the normal.

• Total Internal Reflection (TIR): When light passes from a denser to a less dense medium, there is a critical angle of incidence beyond which refraction becomes impossible. The light is then 100% reflected from the boundary of the media, behaving as if in contact with a perfect mirror. This phenomenon is the basis for the operation of modern optical fibers.

lens.title: 2. Focusing (Lens)
lens.theory:
Idealized optical models assume that lenses focus parallel beams of rays into a single, precise point called the focal point. In reality, spherical lenses exhibit an optical defect known as spherical aberration.

Light rays falling on the peripheral areas of the lens (further from the optical axis) strike the surface at a greater angle. According to Snell's law, they undergo stronger refraction than rays traveling closer to the center. As a result, the common focal point becomes blurred, and the intersecting rays form a characteristic luminous envelope on the plane – a refractive caustic.
lens.descList:
The optical properties of a spherical lens depend directly on its geometry and the material used:

• Caustic curve: The lack of a common focal point for all rays makes it impossible to obtain a sharp image. The light intensity distribution forms a noticeable envelope, the shape of which depends on the lens parameters.

• Dependence on optical density: Materials with a higher IOR (e.g., diamond) exhibit stronger refractive properties. This results in shortening the focal length and shifting the caustic closer to the lens itself, unlike materials with a lower index (e.g., water).

Assumptions and model simplifications:
The simulation presents an idealized, smooth lens in a two-dimensional setup, using monochromatic (single-color) light. In reality, the use of white sunlight would lead to the superposition of another phenomenon – chromatic aberration (dispersion) – which would result in an additional, colorful blur at the edges of the caustic.

cup.title: 3. Reflection: Nephroid & Cardioid
cup.theory:
Caustics are formed not only by refraction but also by reflection. This is governed by the law: the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection. In computer graphics, the reflected ray $\vec{R}$ is calculated as: $$\vec{R} = \vec{D} - 2(\vec{D} \cdot \vec{n})\, \vec{n}$$

The shape of the luminous pattern depends on the geometry of the incoming rays. When the sun (a light source at infinity) casts a parallel beam of rays into a cylindrical cup, a kidney-like shape is formed. Because the rays only reflect off the concave back half of the cylinder, we actually see exactly half of a nephroid (from the Greek nephros – kidney). However, if we place an perfectly isotropic point source exactly on the cup's edge, the rays diverge radially, creating a heart shape on the bottom – a full cardioid. In both cases, these curves act as envelopes – areas where intersecting rays concentrate to form a continuous, bright line.
cup.tip: Do it yourself: Toggle between parallel and point source beams. Notice how changing the wave front completely modifies the caustic's geometry, even though the same reflection formula relative to the wall's normal vector is applied!
cup.descTitle: How does it work in the browser?
cup.descList: Our simulation compares two distinct scenarios of light propagation. In nephroid mode, we use a parallel wave front; in cardioid mode, an infinitely small emission point on the vessel's perimeter. We ignore light refraction at the boundary of mediums to focus purely on the mathematics and geometry of specular reflection.

prism.title: 4. Dispersion (Rainbow)
prism.theory: To understand the rainbow, we must learn about the phenomenon of dispersion. The refractive index $n$ is not a constant – it depends on the wavelength of light $\lambda$. Shorter waves (violet and blue) "slow down" in water slightly more and refract more strongly than long waves (red). This relationship is approximated by the empirical Cauchy's Equation:$$n(\lambda)=A+\frac{B}{\lambda^2}$$Inside a raindrop, white sunlight enters (undergoing dispersion), reflects off its back wall, and exits, creating a colorful caustic at an angle of about 42 degrees. When this phenomenon occurs in millions of drops simultaneously, a rainbow arch lights up in the sky.

controls.title: Dispersion Parameters
controls.mediumDesc: The refractive index for water is not a single number. It changes from 1.331 (for red light) to 1.343 (for violet light). It is precisely this minimal difference that creates the rainbow!

prism.tip: Do it yourself: Set the "Ray Count" slider to just a few. Then very slowly move the angle of incidence slider from left to right. You will notice that at one specific point, the blurred colors suddenly condense, forming a razor-sharp, separated beam. This is exactly where (at the angle of minimum deviation) the Descartes Ray is born!
prism.descTitle: Phenomenon Analysis: Anatomy of a Rainbow
prism.descList:
Increasing the number of rays to the maximum simulates full illumination of the drop. By examining different zones of light incidence, you can observe a full cross-section of optical phenomena:

• Bright background under the rainbow: Rays striking near the center of the drop pass through it and scatter. This explains why the sky under the primary rainbow arch always appears brighter.

• Primary rainbow: In the Descartes strike zone, the beam undergoes massive condensation after one internal reflection, creating a distinct, primary rainbow arch.

• Alexander's band: Between the primary and secondary rainbow zones, there is a range of angles from which no coherent rays return towards the observer. In the real sky (where the sun illuminates the entire drop at once), this phenomenon creates a distinct, dark band separating the two arches.

• Secondary rainbow: Light falling on the opposite part of the drop forms a beam with reversed colors (violet on top, red on the bottom). It is formed from a fraction of rays that managed to reflect inside the drop twice.

• Where does the rest of the light escape? To maintain simulation clarity (and avoid visual clutter), we hid the rays escaping the drop during the first internal reflection – we only draw them for the primary and secondary rainbows. In the next module, using Fresnel equations, we will perform a precise analysis of how much energy escapes and how much remains in the drop!

Model simplifications and Cauchy's equation
In the mathematical formula, constant $A$ is the base refractive index for a given medium, while $B$ is the so-called dispersion coefficient, which determines the strength of color separation. In real water, the difference in the $n$ value between red and violet colors is merely 0.012, resulting in an angular separation only ~2 degrees wide. If hard physical data were implemented, the rainbow on the screen would be a thin thread difficult to spot.

In the presented model, the value of parameter $B$ was deliberately enlarged, artificially stretching the dispersion phenomenon. Thanks to this, the mechanism of separating individual wavelengths is immediately and clearly visible on the screen.

fresnel.title: 5. Fresnel Equations: True Physics of the Rainbow
fresnel.theory:
From previous modules, you already know that Snell's Law ($n_1 \sin(\theta_1) = n_2 \sin(\theta_2)$) determines the direction of refracted light. But how do we know how much energy passes through the barrier and how much reflects? This is where the Fresnel Equations come into play.

They define two key coefficients: $R$ (Reflectance) – the fraction of incident power that undergoes specular reflection, and $T$ (Transmittance) – the fraction of power that passes (escapes) into the second medium. According to the conservation of energy, at any given point $T = 1 - R$. Since sunlight is unpolarized, we calculate the average of the perpendicular ($R_s$) and parallel ($R_p$) polarization. For an air-water boundary ($n_1 \approx 1.0$, $n_2 \approx 1.333$), they look like this:

$$R_s = \left| \frac{n_1 \cos(\theta_1) - n_2 \cos(\theta_2)}{n_1 \cos(\theta_1) + n_2 \cos(\theta_2)} \right|^2$$ $$R_p = \left| \frac{n_1 \cos(\theta_2) - n_2 \cos(\theta_1)}{n_1 \cos(\theta_2) + n_2 \cos(\theta_1)} \right|^2$$ $$R = \frac{1}{2}(R_s + R_p)$$

Why is this crucial? Most educational graphics explaining the rainbow show a ray bouncing off the back wall of a raindrop with 100% reflection. This is a myth! For Total Internal Reflection (TIR) to occur in water, the light must hit the wall at an angle greater than the critical angle $\theta_c$. We can easily calculate this from Snell's Law: $$\theta_c = \arcsin\left(\frac{n_2}{n_1}\right) = \arcsin\left(\frac{1.0}{1.333}\right) \approx 48.6^\circ$$

A classic, sharp rainbow is formed in tiny raindrops (under 1 mm) where surface tension dominates, maintaining an almost perfectly spherical shape. In such a perfect sphere, geometry strictly guarantees that an incoming external ray will never hit the internal wall at an angle greater than the aforementioned 48.6°. TIR is simply geometrically impossible here – the vast majority of the energy ($T$) escapes straight through, and the rainbow is formed only from the reflected remnants of energy ($R$).

Fun Fact: Very large raindrops flatten out due to air resistance. Their distorted geometry can occasionally trigger TIR, but due to the resulting optical chaos, they cannot form a distinct rainbow.
fresnel.tip: Do it yourself: Toggle colors and observe the subtle changes in the table – violet light refracts slightly stronger and undergoes a minimally stronger reflection (R)! Move the angle slider from -90° to 90°. Notice that even at an extreme 89°, the internal impact angle will never exceed ~48.6°. At exactly 90°, the ray will "graze" the edge, and transmission to the inside will drop to 0%.
fresnel.descTitle: Anatomy of the simulation and data reading
fresnel.descList:
Our live simulation solves vector-based Fresnel equations, proving how inefficient a "mirror" the inside of a raindrop truly is.

How to read the data?
To show the actual, drastic loss of light intensity, the table displays the global % of the initial solar energy. Because of this, the Reflection (R) and Transmission (T) values in a given row do not sum up to 100% – their sum always equals the Energy In value (i.e., what managed to reach that specific point of impact).

On the other hand, the labels rendered directly on the drawing animation show the local perspective. For each specific point of impact, they display the split proportion (summing up exactly to 100%), illustrating the pure boundary physics at that moment.

gpu.title: 5. Global Illumination and Caustics (3D Simulation)
gpu.theory:
Previous models relied on analytically tracking the geometry of individual rays in an isolated 2D system. In a three-dimensional environment, optical phenomena become incomparably more complex. The boundary between media (e.g., water surface) is rarely perfectly flat – it is a dynamic structure. Every single wave acts as an asymmetrical, fluid lens that focuses and scatters passing light in a fraction of a second.

To recreate these behaviors in real time, it is necessary to account for the trajectories of countless rays. This phenomenon illustrates how elementary laws of optics, occurring en masse across the entire liquid surface, generate complex, multidimensional light structures.
gpu.descList:
Recreating a 3D environment allows for the simultaneous observation of many optical phenomena discussed in previous sections:

• Dynamic refractive caustics: The rippled liquid surface acts as an infinite grid of moving microlenses. The phenomenon of spherical aberration (previously seen in a single lens) occurs massively here, creating a dense, constantly changing network of bright focal curves and dark, underexposed areas on the pool floor.

• Complex image refraction: The shape of a sphere submerged in water undergoes visual distortion. Light rays reflected from the object refract upon exiting the water at the uneven wave surface, in full compliance with the 3D application of Snell's Law.

• Chromatic aberration on the floor: Similar to the rainbow phenomenon, water exhibits a dependence of the refractive index on the wavelength of light. This results in dispersion at the edges of focused light beams (especially noticeable on the brightest caustic bands), generating characteristic, colorful fringes.

• Computational optimization: Physically correct tracking of millions of photons (Ray Tracing / Path Tracing) is an extremely demanding process for logic systems. In interactive 3D applications, these effects are simulated using specialized shading programs (shaders), which utilize the parallel power of GPUs to calculate approximate light paths and generate caustic textures in a matter of milliseconds.
